paragraphs.text: Quincy and Becca sat in the dark classroom, fanning themselves. The other students had all gone home because of the blackout, but Becca's parents couldn't pick her up early. Quincy had forgotten his house key, so he was stuck at school too, until his mom came. Mrs. DeWitt sat by the window, grading papers.
"At least we got to skip the debates today," Quincy said.
"Don't worry," Mrs. DeWitt said with a smile. "We'll hold the debates tomorrow."
"I like to debate," Becca said. "But it's so hard to prepare when we don't know the topic ahead of time."
Mrs. DeWitt nodded. "It is, but I want you to think of strong arguments on the spot. Everyone has opinions—people should know how to support their opinions."
"I definitely have an opinion about this blackout," Quincy groaned. "Being without power is boring and hot!"
"The utility company asked residents to conserve energy during the heat wave so we wouldn't have a blackout," Mrs. DeWitt said. "But people must be using more power than the system can handle."

Becca had been studying renewable energy in science. She remembered something that she had read. "People use less household electricity now than they did ten years ago. Appliances and technology are more energy efficient."
"Oh?" Mrs. DeWitt said. "Interesting . . . "

"Well, I think we need more power plants to produce more energy," Quincy burst out. "The problem is, most power plants burn fossil fuels like coal, oil, or natural gas. And that's bad for the environment."
"So what's the solution?" Mrs. DeWitt asked.

"More people should use solar power!" Becca declared. "It's clean, renewable energy. In fact, enough solar energy hits Earth in one hour to provide all the power we need for a year. With solar, families could cover all their household electricity needs."
"Solar panels are expensive, and so is installing them," Quincy pointed out. "Plus, the panels aren't efficient. Only some of the sun's energy that hits them gets converted into electricity."
"What's your idea, Quincy?" Mrs. DeWitt asked.
Quincy thought for a moment. "Wind and water are renewable sources of energy, unlike fossil fuels. And they don't produce air pollution. We could build more wind turbines and dams."

Becca shook her head. "Dams take up a lot of space and disrupt the environment. Even wind farms disturb the land's surface. These forms of power can only be built in places with water or wind." She grinned. "Solar panels don't disrupt the environment. And they can be installed anywhere the sun shines—like on peoples' roofs."

"True, but people need a lot of panels to cover their entire usage. They also need a battery system to store energy for when the sun isn't shining," Quincy said. "Dams and wind farms can produce larger amounts of electricity than solar."
"I see your point," Becca said. "But if more people use solar, we could reduce our need for big power plants."
"Wouldn't it be better to wait until costs go down and the technology is more efficient?" Quincy asked.
"Nope! We need more solar power now," Becca said. "The more people use solar, the more costs will go down and the technology will improve."
Mrs. DeWitt began to clap. "Great job, you two."
The kids looked at her, confused.
"With what?" Becca asked.
"With your arguments about renewable energy," the teacher said. "You each earned an A on tomorrow's debate assignment."
"Yes!" Quincy sat back with a grin.
But Becca leaned forward. "Who won?"
"It was a tie," Mrs. DeWitt said. "You both presented clear opinions and supported them with strong evidence. That's exactly what skilled debaters do."
Just then the classroom phone buzzed. Mrs. DeWitt picked it up and spoke to the school secretary for a moment.
"Quincy, your mom is waiting at the main office."
"Great!" He grabbed his things and headed toward the door.
"Stay cool!" Becca said.
"I will." Quincy grinned. "At home we're prepared for blackouts. We have backup solar power!"

It's not easy being a plant. Plants are often on the dinner menu for hungry animals and insects. Reproducing can be a challenge. Sometimes there aren't enough nutrients in the soil for plants to eat. So how have plants survived? They've adapted! Over millions of years, they've found unique ways to survive.

Plants can't run from insects or other animals that are trying to eat them. But some plants can hide. They don't jump behind trees or scurry under rocks. Instead they use camouflage to hide from predators. These plants have a natural shape or color that helps them blend in with their surroundings.

The Lithops plant has an amazing way to hide itself—it looks like stones! These plants can be found in southern Africa where it is very dry. Lithops is a succulent. Succulents are plants with thick leaves that can store a lot of water. Cactuses and aloe plants are also succulents. Succulents usually live in deserts, where water is scarce.

During the rainy season, Lithops ' leaves push up from the soil. They soak up lots of water and become round like stones. Since the leaves look like rocks, animals leave them alone, letting them hide in plain sight! Lithops ' leaves have a small slit on top. When blooms appear, they grow from the slit. It looks just like the blooms are growing between two stones.

Some plants don't try to hide. The titan arum is too big to use camouflage to blend in. Its blooms are usually about two-and-a-half meters tall. That makes it one of the largest flowers in the world. This plant has a special adaptation to help it with reproduction: it stinks! The titan arum's enormous blossoms smell like dung or rotting flesh. This is really gross to humans, but it's not gross to flies.

Titan arum plants live in Indonesia's warm, wet rainforests. When it blooms, the stems of the plant grow warm. That helps spread its smell far and wide. When flies smell the blossoms, they come and walk on the flowers. Bits of pollen stick to their legs. Then the flies travel to other titan arum flowers, spreading the pollen and helping the titan arum reproduce. Even though the plant blooms only once every few years, this stinky adaptation is key to the species' survival.

Like humans, plants need to eat to survive. Most plants simply get their nutrients from soil. But soil in environments like swamps and marshes has few nutrients. So certain plants that live in these environments have become carnivores. That's right—they eat meat! Some carnivorous plants have sticky leaves that trap insects that land on them. Others have slippery leaves. Insects slide down the leaves into a pool of the plants' digestive juices. Usually carnivorous plants eat insects, but sometimes they eat small frogs or mammals.

Venus flytraps are probably the most well-known carnivorous plants. They live in the swamps of the southeastern United States. They have pairs of leaves with small hairs on them. When an insect touches these hairs, the two leaves snap shut, trapping the insect inside. Then the plant digests the insect. This can take a flytrap a week or longer. But eventually it gets the nutrients it needs.

Staying safe, reproducing, and getting enough nutrients can be challenging for plants. But plants are tough and have adapted to survive. The next time you see a plant, take a look and see how it has adapted to its environment. You might find something pretty cool—or weird!
Kaitlyn was practicing her pitching at the baseball field. She reached into her bucket for another ball. Suddenly— beep, beep, beep!
A big truck backed slowly onto the field.
"Hey!" Kaitlyn thought. "What's that doing here?"
A man got out of the truck. "Sorry," he said. "We need to set up here for tonight's fireworks display. You'll have to move somewhere else."
"The Fourth of July show is still hours away," Kaitlyn said. "Can't I practice my pitching some more?"
"I'm afraid not," the man said. "It takes several hours to set up a fireworks display."
By now more men had arrived. They were moving wooden racks and boxes onto the field.
Kaitlyn sighed. She looked closely at a rack. It held short plastic pipes. "Those are fireworks?"

"Nope," the man said. "Those are cannons that shoot the fireworks into the sky." He opened a box and took out a brown object wrapped in plastic. It was about the size of a baseball and looked like a little bomb. "This is a firework shell."
"What's inside of it?" Kaitlyn asked.

"I'll explain," said the man. He set the shell gently back into the box. Then he bent down and drew a big circle in the dirt. "A shell is filled with little balls of gunpowder. Pyrotechnicians, like me, call these balls 'stars.'" He picked up some baseballs and formed a pattern inside the circle with them. "The pattern of the stars gives a firework its shape."
"What gives a firework its color?" Kaitlyn asked.
"Magic!" The man laughed. Kaitlyn didn't. She really wanted to know the answer!

"Well, the magic of science," the man added quickly. "Pyrotechnicians add chemicals to the gunpowder stars. When these chemicals burn, they make different colors. Like chemicals containing copper, for example—can you guess what color they make when they burn?"
Kaitlyn pulled a penny from her pocket and glanced at it. "Orangish brown?"
"Nope!" the man said. "Chemicals with copper make blue. Chemicals with calcium make orange."

Next the man drew a square attached to the circle. "There's even more gunpowder here at the bottom of the shell." He drew a long line from the center of the circle. "This is the fuse. It's a string that lights the shell. When the shell is in the cannon, the fuse lights the gunpowder at the bottom of the shell. That explosion pushes the shell out of the cannon and into the air."
"The shell doesn't burst inside the cannon?"
"Nope. The fuse continues to burn in the air. Finally it explodes the shell and lights the stars. That's when you see the firework in the sky."
"Awesome," Kaitlyn said. "Hmm. I guess you do have a lot to do before tonight."
"Right. It's a big show with many fireworks! And we have to work carefully and safely. Working with fireworks is very dangerous."
The man helped Kaitlyn gather her baseballs. "Are you going to watch the display tonight?" he asked, dropping the last baseball into her bucket.
Kaitlyn smiled. "I can't wait!"
It was the day of the winter science fair. Stella sat at a table with a jar of snow. There was a display with information about snowflakes behind her.
Her friend's mom came over to the table. "Hey, Stella. What's your project about?"
Stella smiled. "Hi, Mrs. Singer. I did some research on snow."
"That sounds interesting," Mrs. Singer said. "So, are you a snow expert now?"
Stella grinned. "I'm not sure yet. But I learned how snow forms."
By now a couple of other adults stood nearby.
"Let's hear about it," the man said.

"Okay," Stella said. "First the outdoor temperature must be 0 degrees Celsius or below. That freezes the water vapor in the air. The frozen vapor then attaches to specks of dust and pollen. When this happens, tiny ice crystals form. Like all crystals, these have flat sides and sharp corners.
"Some of the ice crystals stick together, forming clumps of crystals. They grow bigger and bigger. Eventually all these crystals fall to the ground as snow."
"Hmm." Mrs. Singer rubbed her chin. "So, snowflakes are just clumps of ice crystals that are stuck together?"
Stella nodded. "Some snowflakes have up to two hundred ice crystals."
"Whoa!" the woman said. "Can you tell us what makes the ice crystals fall out of the clouds?"
"Yes," Stella said. "But the ice crystals don't really fall out of the clouds. The ice crystals are the clouds. They are what clouds are made of. "
"Oh," the woman said.

"The bunches of ice crystals get heavy," Stella said. "That's when they fall to the ground as snow. It's the same thing with rain. Water vapor turns into water droplets. They join together. And when the droplets are heavy enough, they fall as rain."
Mrs. Singer pointed to the poster. "Tell us about those pretty snowflakes."

"Sure." Stella stood up so everyone could see the poster better. "My poster shows all the basic shapes of snowflakes. Some are shaped like stars, needles, or plates. Others have little branches. Most snowflakes have six sides or six points. But every snowflake is different. In fact, you'll probably never find two that are exactly the same."
"Huh," the man said. "Why are they all so different?"

"Because ice crystals stick together in lots of different ways," Stella said. "Other things affect their shape too—like the air's temperature and its moisture levels. When there's just a little moisture in the air, snowflakes are shaped like flat plates. They're shaped like stars when there's more moisture in the air."
"Very interesting!" the man said. "I never knew that."
"Oh!" Stella said suddenly. "I just remembered one other thing. You know how snow looks white? Well, that's only because of how light reflects off all the crystals. Snow is actually clear."
"Wow, Stella." Mrs. Singer smiled at her. "You are an expert on snow."
"I guess I am." Stella smiled too. "To me, snowflakes are amazing!"
I'm at the airport with my family. We're taking a trip to Vietnam to visit my grandparents. Vietnam is halfway around the world from here. That means it'll be a very long flight!

Flying is fun. I like being up in the sky and looking down at the clouds. But do you know what I'd love to do one day? I want to look down at Earth—from outer space! And soon it could be possible because space travel is changing fast.

For many years only astronauts traveled to space. But today, private companies are building spaceships so that others can visit space too. These companies have created a whole new market called space tourism.
Space tourists pay money to travel above Earth in spaceships. So far there are mainly two kinds of space tourism.

Suborbital space tourists take short trips. People travel about 97 kilometers above Earth, to the edge of outer space. There's no gravity there, so they feel weightless for a few minutes. They also get an amazing view of Earth. They see its curved surface, outlined by the thin blue line of the atmosphere. Countless stars fill the background. A suborbital trip lasts between ten minutes and a couple of hours.

Orbital space tourists go much higher, traveling about 320 kilometers above Earth. This is high enough to enter Earth's orbit. This is the zone where an object will orbit around Earth. Some tourists go around the planet a few times. Others visit the International Space Station or ISS. Orbital trips last a few days or longer.
Private companies are also planning to build space hotels. These hotels will be like space stations that orbit Earth. It's so cool—people will be able to take vacations in space!

Several countries have big plans for building in space too. Many want to build bases on the moon. People will live and work on the bases. And they can be used to help scientists explore deep space. For example, missions to Mars could be launched from moon bases. Someday there might be whole colonies on Mars. If that happens, lots of people will be visiting space!

Space travel is exciting, but it's also dangerous. Equipment can break down, causing deadly accidents. And human bodies aren't used to being in space. Space has high levels of radiation that can cause diseases. Also, without gravity, human bones and muscles grow weaker.

Right now space tourism is only for very rich people. A ticket for a suborbital flight costs hundreds of thousands of dollars. Orbital space tourism costs even more. In 2022, people who visited the ISS paid over $50 million each!
I can't wait to see Vietnam. Someday I want to tour the moon too. After that, I'll travel to Mars. My space trips will be amazing—and expensive. I'd better start saving my money now!

Antarctica is a huge, cold, inhospitable place at the bottom of the earth. Who would want to go there? Lots of people, in fact! Explorers and scientists have always been drawn to this mysterious continent. Nations have claimed pieces of the ice-covered land. Now it's even a popular destination for tourists.

Antarctica is the fifth-largest continent on earth. It's also the coldest place on earth. Yes, it's even colder than the Arctic! The lowest temperatures in the world have been recorded here—below -90 degrees Celsius. Antarctica's fierce winds can make it feel even colder!

Most of the land is covered by the Antarctic Ice Sheet, which contains 90 percent of the world's ice. It's a dramatic, glacial landscape with icebergs breaking off into the sea. The ice averages over two kilometers in thickness. Hidden under its snowy surface are deep, dangerous cracks.

Ice isn't the only feature of the landscape. Rock and soil cover a small part of the land—less than a half percent. There are mountains and volcanoes too. And Antarctica is actually a desert! That's because it receives only about 150 millimeters of precipitation each year. Of course that usually falls as snow.

Under these harsh conditions, there isn't much plant life. Mosses and algae are some of the few plants that can survive. But there is abundant animal life. Fish, whales, seals, and penguins all call Antarctica their home.

Antarctica is the only continent without a native human population. Yet people were fascinated by it even before it was discovered. Before the age of exploration in the fifteenth century, Europeans were sure they knew what the world looked like—even though they hadn't seen most of it yet! They decided that the northern and southern hemispheres contained the same amount of land. Sixteenth-century maps showed a huge landmass in the far south. Mapmakers didn't know what this land looked like or exactly where it was. But that didn't stop them from drawing it!

In 1773 Captain James Cook became the first explorer to sail into the Antarctic Circle. By the 1820s several explorers had seen Antarctica. During the early twentieth century, men risked their lives exploring the continent. Who would be the first to reach the South Pole? In 1911 two expeditions raced to the pole. Roald Amundsen of Norway arrived in December. He was followed by Robert Falcon Scott of the United Kingdom a month later. Sadly, Scott and four men died on the way back.
By the late 1950s, several countries had established research stations in Antarctica. Seven countries even claimed parts of Antarctica, and some claims overlapped. But no one was actually in charge.

Scientists didn't want Antarctica to become a place of conflict. They wanted people to work together peacefully. So the Antarctic Treaty was signed in 1959. The treaty doesn't allow military activity or nuclear testing and disposal in Antarctica. More than fifty nations have now signed the treaty.

Today approximately thirty countries run seventy-five research stations. Scientists study everything from marine life to astronomy to climate change. No one lives permanently in Antarctica. Scientists come and go. Their numbers are the greatest from December to March—summer in Antarctica.

Scientists aren't the only people who visit. More than 45,000 tourists arrive each year to see the ice and wildlife. If they're hoping to see polar bears, they return home disappointed. Polar bears live in the Arctic. But they may see emperor penguins. These birds can be found in only one place on earth—Antarctica!

It was the navy's Fleet Week. The bay was full of ships for people to see and visit. Orson stood with his cousin Nick on top of a long black submarine. Nick was a sailor who worked aboard this underwater vessel.
"What does this submarine do?" Orson asked.
"The navy uses submarines to help protect our country," Nick said. "Most of our missions are for military research. Ready to see inside?"
Orson shivered. The sub had no windows. It seemed scary.
Nick climbed down the ladder inside the hatch, the round opening that led into the sub. "Come on down," he called.
Orson cautiously stepped onto the ladder's first rung. "Will the sub sink while we're on board?"

"Subs control when they submerge," Nick assured him as they climbed down the ladder. "Tanks filled with air help them float. To submerge, we pump water into the tanks. That makes the sub heavier, so it goes down."
"How does it get back up?"
"We fill the tanks with air again to make it float." Nick grinned at him. "We won't submerge today."
Orson reached the bottom of the ladder. "Why is it so cramped in here? The sub looks huge on the outside."

"Nuclear subs are big. This one is over ninety meters long, but the power plant and equipment take up most of the space," said Nick. "The 135 crew members get any room that's left." He laughed. "Some subs, like the ones they use for scientific research, are powered with oil. Oil-powered subs must surface every few days. Nuclear subs can stay underwater for months."
"Don't you run out of water and air when the sub stays underwater that long?"
"We make our own fresh water and air."
"We made fresh water in school!" Orson said. "We boiled salt water and saved the condensed steam. Is that what you do?"
"Exactly," said Nick. "We make enough water for crew members to drink and take a three-minute shower every day. Most of the water, though, is used to cool equipment."
"How do you make air?"
"We take oxygen from water. And we can reuse existing air by getting rid of the carbon dioxide people breathe out."
"Cool," Orson said.
Nick led Orson through rooms filled with computers. "We navigate with GPS on the surface, but GPS doesn't work underwater. So we navigate by keeping track of our direction and speed."
"How do you keep the sub from crashing into things?"
"We use sound. We listen for sounds from other ships. We also use a device called sonar. It bounces sound off objects to detect and locate them."
"That's what dolphins do!" Orson said.
They climbed down a narrow stairway. Here beds were stacked three-high along the walls.
"This is the crew's quarters." Nick pointed to a small drawer under one bed. "I keep all my stuff here."
"Everything?" Orson had a room full of stuff at home. "What do you do all day?"

"I'm on watch for eight hours. That's when I'm helping to operate the sub. When I'm not on watch, I still have to work to help clean and maintain the sub. We get some free time too. Then I sleep for eight hours."
Suddenly the sub rocked. "Whoa!" Orson said.
"Don't worry," Nick said. "Waves rock subs on the surface, but it's smooth sailing underwater."
"I believe you." Orson smiled. "Living underwater seems like living in a spaceship! But I think I like living on land better!"
Kevin, Nadine, and Dad looked at the huge tree lying in their backyard.
"I can't believe the storm blew our tree down," said Nadine. Tears filled her eyes.
"I loved climbing that tree," Kevin said sadly.
Dad sighed. "This old oak tree was here when my dad built this house."

A truck pulled into the driveway. Workers with chainsaws got out. The workers cut off the small branches. Then they cut into the thick trunk. Sawdust filled the air. With a giant crack, the trunk broke in half.
"It has rings of wood inside!" said Nadine.
"Most trees add one ring every year," said Dad. "We can count the rings to find the tree's age."
Kevin and Nadine took turns counting.
"Our tree was 213 years old!" Nadine said.
"That's right, and it has a tale to tell," said a lady behind them.
"You must be Dr. Learner," said Dad.
She smiled at the kids.
"Dr. Learner is taking a slab for the Tree Ring Lab. It's at the University of Arizona," said Dad.

Dr. Learner explained that the Tree Ring Lab had two million tree samples. "Trees build a picture of the earth's history," she said. She pointed to a thin ring in the trunk. "This year had little rain, so your tree did not grow very much."
"Cool!" said Nadine, pointing to a thick ring. "This year was rainy."
"Trees are like a weather calendar!" said Kevin.

"More than that," said Dr. Learner. She pointed to a twisted ring. "This scar shows that something unusual happened—likely a fire. Trees can tell us about big events. A tree would grow less if a hurricane blew off its leaves. Or if a volcano erupted."
Kevin laughed. "People would remember a volcano eruption!"
Dr. Learner showed them a picture of a tree slab. It was twice as tall as a man. "This tree grew from 212 to 1913."
"Whoa! That's 1,701 years!" said Nadine.
Kevin shrugged. "Okay, maybe trees are better than people at remembering things."
Dr. Learner smiled. "The oldest living tree is five thousand years old."
Nadine's eyes grew wide. "How do you know that without cutting it down?"
"We use a tool that drills a tiny hole," said Dr. Learner. "It doesn't hurt the tree."
The workers finished. The backyard was quiet. It looked strange without the tall tree.
Nadine spied something near the fence. "Look! Our tree had a baby!"
The family hurried over. The tree was tiny.
"I wonder what stories this tree will tell in the future," said Kevin.
"I don't think you'll find out," said Dad. "But maybe your grandchildren or your great-grandchildren will."
"Look, Dad!" Lila said, waving a flyer. "The amusement park is having a roller coaster design contest. First prize is two tickets for the first ride on the new coaster!"
Dad leaned back and pretended he was riding a roller coaster. "I love when I'm pushed back in the seat."
"It only feels like you're being pushed back. The seat is really pushing you forward."
Dad laughed. "You sure know your stuff!"

Lila started drawing ideas. First she drew a lift hill. She knew that roller coasters didn't have motors. The cars gained speed as gravity pulled them down from the top of the lift hill. This momentum would carry the cars through the rest of the roller coaster.

"My hill looks too short," Lila thought. "The cars won't have enough momentum to go through loops or over hills." She made the hill a bit taller. If she made it too tall, the cars would gain too much speed. Then the ride would be uncomfortable or dangerous.
After the lift hill, Lila added loops, hills, and curves. "Yes!" Lila declared. She was almost ready to build a model!
As Dad drove to the park, Lila practiced explaining her model. "Gravity pulls you down at the top of the loop, but the momentum keeps pushing you forward."
"That gives you the weightless feeling?" Dad asked.
"Exactly."
Dad parked. As Lila started to get out of the car, the box slipped from her hands.
Lila gasped as her model crashed onto the pavement. "It's ruined! What am I going to do? Judging starts soon!"
Dad helped her pick up the pieces. "It's not too bad. You'll think of something."

In the waiting room, Lila examined the other contestants' designs. Some wouldn't work, but others were good. She stared at the pieces of her model in the box. "Hey!" she thought suddenly. "Maybe I can put the pieces together as I explain my model!"
Soon it was Lila's turn. In the judging room, Lila put the lift hill on the table. "A cable pulls the cars to the top."
Next she put the loop on the table. "From the lift hill, the cars should have enough speed to go through this loop."
"Why isn't the loop round?" judge number one asked.
"A round loop makes the cars go the same speed all around. This teardrop shape slows the speed on the sides of the loop to make the ride more comfortable."
The judges nodded. Lila's plan was working! But as she took the last piece from the box, her heart sank. Part of the track was twisted upside down!
"Interesting," judge number two said.
"This isn't how I designed it," Lila admitted. "I dropped the model in the parking lot."
"Do you think it would work on a real coaster?" judge number one asked.
"Hmm. I think the momentum coming out of the loop would carry the cars through the twist."
Lila sat nervously in the waiting room. "I couldn't answer the twist question."
"I'm sure you did well," Dad assured her.
Finally the judges called everyone back in.
"The winner is Lila King!" judge number one announced. "For her good model and her great knowledge of roller coaster physics!"
Judge number two shook Lila's hand and handed her the tickets.
"My company has a summer camp for future engineers," he said. "You should think about attending."
Lila grinned. "I'll definitely look into it—after I ride the new coaster!"
Mom popped her head into my room. "Your room is clean!"
"I'm building my computer," I told her. "You have to build a computer in a clean space. No dust or cat hair."
Dad came in and sat on my bed. He looked impressed when he saw the computer parts spread out on my desk. "So what do you do first?"
"This is the power supply." I held up a black box with cords running out. "First I'll put it in the computer's case so I can plug the computer in."
"Be careful!" said Mom.
"I'll keep everything unplugged while I'm building," I said as I screwed the power supply into the case. "Next I have to work with the motherboard." I held up the board.
Mom chuckled. "It looks more like a 'robot' board than a 'mother' board."

"A motherboard is like the computer's nervous system. Other parts plug into it, and the motherboard lets the parts communicate. The motherboard makes sure the information in the computer gets to where it needs to go."
"Your mother makes sure everyone in our family gets to where they need to go," said Dad.
Mom laughed.
I picked up a small square package. "This is the central processing unit, or CPU. The CPU does all of the computer's work. It's like the computer's brain."
"That's a pretty thin brain!" said Dad. "How can it remember anything?"
"The CPU isn't exactly like a person's brain," I explained. "It does the thinking for the computer, but it doesn't actually store information. There are two other pieces of hardware for that."
I pointed to a metal box. "The hard drive is where the computer stores all of its information. When you save something, it's stored on the hard drive."

Then I held up a rectangular piece. "This is RAM. That stands for random access memory. RAM is where the computer puts information while it's working on it. I'm putting in extra RAM so I can work on several things at the same time."
"I could use extra memory!" Dad laughed.
I attached the RAM and CPU to the motherboard. Then I carefully placed the motherboard in the case.
"Is the computer ready?" asked Mom.
"Not yet." I pointed out spots on the motherboard. "These places are where you add parts for sound and graphics. I got a good graphics card for playing games."
I put the remaining parts into place and connected my monitor to the computer. "Let's plug it in now," I said, crossing my fingers for luck.
Dad plugged the computer into a power strip, and I switched it on. We heard the computer start up, and then numbers scrolled up the screen. Mom and Dad cheered and I let out a sigh of relief.
"Can you surf the internet now?" Mom asked.
"Not yet. This is just the hardware," I said. "I still have to install software—the programs and code that tell the computer what to do."
"Can you write code too?" asked Dad teasingly.
I smiled. "That's my next project."

Pedro zigzagged around Great-Aunt Luisa's dark front yard, holding his phone up. He was trying to get a stronger signal. Great-Aunt Luisa lived in the countryside, where there wasn't much to do. Pedro was staying with her for a whole month.
"Are you taking pictures of the moon?" a voice called.
Pedro spotted a girl in a neighbor's yard. "No. I was just trying to get a signal." He glanced upward. The nearly full moon looked much brighter than it looked at home in the city.
The girl smiled. "I'm Luna. Want to take a look through my telescope?"
"Sure." Pedro walked over to where Luna had set up her telescope. "I've never seen the moon through a telescope before."
"One day I'd like to see it up close." Luna's eyes shone. "My dream is to become an astronaut and explore the moon."
"You sure like the moon a lot. Is it because your name means 'moon' in Spanish?" Pedro asked teasingly.
Luna grinned. "It could be. Hey! There's a full moon tomorrow. Want to watch it with me?"
Pedro smiled. "Definitely!"
The next night Pedro met Luna in her yard. "The moon is a different shape tonight," he said.

Luna giggled. "The moon doesn't really change shape, you know. The sun lights up the moon's surface. As the moon orbits around Earth, the amount of the sunlit surface we can see changes. These changes are the phases of the moon."
"Aha," Pedro said. "How long does it take for the moon to orbit Earth?"
"About four weeks—one lunar month," Luna said.
"Oh. Is tonight the start of a lunar month?"
"Nope! The full moon is halfway through a lunar month," Luna explained. "The new moon is the start of a lunar month. But it's a confusing name."
"Why?" Pedro asked.
"Because that's when the unlit surface of the moon is facing Earth. We can't see the moon then."
"That should be called a 'no moon' then!" Pedro grinned.

Luna laughed. "After a new moon, the moon waxes—or looks like it gets bigger. A few days later, it's a waxing crescent. One week after the new moon is the first-quarter moon. That's when half of the moon's surface is visible from Earth."
"Why is it a quarter moon if half of it is visible?"
"Because it's one quarter of the way through the lunar month," Luna said. "Finally after another week, we have a full moon, like this one. Are you enjoying it?"
Pedro put his eye to the telescope again. "It's awesome!"
For the next few nights, Pedro and Luna watched the moon slowly seem to disappear.
"It's waning. This is a waning gibbous," Luna explained, pointing to the football-shaped moon. "In a few days, we'll see the third-quarter moon."
Over a week later it was a new moon, and the sky was moonless. Soon the moon reappeared, and the waxing moon slowly grew again.
One night, under a full moon, Pedro's mom arrived to pick him up.
"Hey, Pedro!" Luna called as Pedro put his stuff into Mom's car. Luna was holding a big, long box. "I thought you might like this."
"Whoa! I can't take that," Pedro said. It was her telescope!
Luna grinned. "I'm getting a new one soon. So please take this one."
"Thanks!" Pedro said. "That's really generous, Luna. I'm sorry that I don't have anything for you though."
"That's okay." Luna smiled. "Just promise me we can moon-gaze together when I visit the city."
Pedro smiled back. "Deal!"

Before 1980, Mount St. Helens, in Washington, was just another volcano in the Ring of Fire. That's the huge circle of volcanoes that ring the Pacific Ocean. The volcano had not erupted in over a hundred years. It was green and rich with wildlife. Spirit Lake, below the mountain, was full of fish and plants. But then this volcano woke up!

Hot melted rock, called magma, had created lots of gas deep underground. This gas had built up, causing pressure within the volcano. On May 18, 1980, an earthquake struck the area—and Mount St. Helens finally erupted.

When the volcano exploded, its entire north side collapsed. This created the biggest landslide in modern history. Lava, which is magma that has reached the surface, blasted out of the mountain. The lava mixed with rock, ash, and melted snow. It flowed over the landscape. Clouds of hot gases and rocks burst out too. They knocked down entire forests.
The violent eruption left a huge crater at the top of the mountain—nearly three kilometers wide. Mount St. Helens was now four hundred meters shorter than before the eruption!
This wasn't the most serious damage. Fifty-seven people died in the eruption. Roads, bridges, and hundreds of homes were destroyed.

Right after the eruption, scientists began to study the scene. Ash and volcanic rock covered most of the landscape. Spirit Lake was filled with ash and rock too. Broken trees covered the surface of the lake. There was nothing alive in sight. The entire area looked as lifeless as the moon!

Scientists believed decades would pass before animals and plants returned to the area. Yet only three months later, scientists spotted something incredible. A gopher was digging out of its tunnel! The animal had stayed safe underground during the dangerous eruption. By the next spring, a plant was growing! After ten years, plants had grown back and animals had returned. Plankton and plants filled Spirit Lake again. Life had returned to the mountain.

Meanwhile the volcano hadn't exactly fallen back to sleep. After the eruption, lava continued to build up at the crater's floor. It rose and rose. By 1986 the lava had formed a dome 270 meters high. Then the mountain grew mostly quiet again. Once in a while, the mountain rumbled. There were even small explosions. But none of this activity was very serious.

In 2004 ash and steam clouds rose once more from the crater. Rocks as big as buildings pushed up from the crater floor. What was happening now? No one knew. But by 2007 the mountain went back to sleep. Scientists think that the volcano may have run out of gas.

Today earthquakes and rumblings continue to occur near Mount St. Helens. The good news is that scientists have learned a lot since the 1980 eruption. These lessons will help them to make better predictions about future eruptions. No one knows exactly when Mount St. Helens will wake up again. But when it does, people are more likely to be prepared.
Jimmy's family was on their way to a beach vacation. As they drove along, his parents and twin brother Jason were talking excitedly.
"I'm going to walk on the beach every morning," Mom said.
"I'm going fishing," Dad said.
"Can we go to the amusement park?" Jason asked. "There's a new roller coaster—Motion Monster."
Jimmy stayed quiet.
"What's wrong, Jimmy?" Mom asked.
He shrugged. "Nothing."
"I know what's wrong!" Jason grinned. "This is a long car ride. He's worried he's going to throw up!"
"I brought some stuff, in case you do feel carsick." Mom held up a bag. "I've got peppermint gum, ginger candy, wristbands, and even some medicine. One of these treatments might help."
Jimmy sighed. "Why do I get carsick anyway?"
"It's called motion sickness," Mom said. "It comes from your ears and your eyes having a disagreement."
"Kind of like . . ." Jimmy looked at Jason. "Twins disagreeing?"

"Not exactly," Mom said. "Motion sickness occurs when one sense detects motion, but another one does not. For example, if you're reading in the car, your eyes think you're staying still. Meanwhile your ears detect motion, and the two senses clash."
"So your brain gets different messages," Dad added. "And you start to sweat or feel sick to your stomach."
"I never get carsick," Jason bragged.
"Doctors aren't sure why some people get motion sickness and others do not," Mom said. "But it's very common, especially among kids."

"Grandma gets motion sickness on airplanes," Dad said. "My friend Shin gets seasick on boats. He eats ginger before he goes sailing—that's what Chinese fishermen have done for centuries. It calms your stomach. Another trick is to stare at the horizon when you're seasick."
"Uh-oh . . ." Jimmy could see that their car was approaching a curvy road.
"Here." Mom handed him the gum. "The doctor said peppermint is good for stomachaches. Roll down your window for fresh air. Don't read or look at a screen."
Jimmy followed his mom's advice. As the car drove along the road, he chewed gum and closed his eyes.
"How's it going?" Mom asked.
He took a deep breath. "Good! I feel fine!"
The week at the beach flew by. One cloudy day the family went to the amusement park.
"Whoa, check it out!" Jason pointed to Motion Monster. It was an enormous roller coaster with steep hills and huge loops. "Let's go!"
The twins raced over to the ride and hopped into the first car. Minutes later they began going up the first slope.
"Ahh!" Jason screamed as they flew downward.
Jimmy threw his arms up. "Whee! This is awesome!"
But when he looked over at his twin, he saw Jason clutching his stomach.
"What's wrong?" Jimmy asked. But he already knew the answer. Jason had motion sickness!
Isabel opened her suitcase and started to unpack. Her father had already left for a meeting.
"This is going to be so boring," she mumbled. "How can you have fun when it's dark and cold all the time?"

Isabel and her father lived in Florida. But for the next month, her father was working at a university in Tromsø, Norway. The city was north of the Arctic Circle, and they had arrived during the polar night. Because of Earth's tilt, polar regions receive almost no sunlight during this time. In Tromsø this lasts from November through January—three whole months!
Just then Isabel heard a knock. It was the university student who lived next door.
"Hello," Erik said with a friendly smile. "Ready for your tour of Tromsø? Dress warmly—it's cold outside!"
Isabel forced a polite smile in return. "Ugh," she thought. "Right now my friends are probably at the beach!"
Isabel followed Erik as he pointed out restaurants, theaters, and shops. She spotted a group of kids wearing ski gear.
"Are they going skiing?"
Erik grinned. "Why does that surprise you?"
"It's dark outside! Isn't it dangerous to ski now?"
"There are lights on the slopes. And it's fun to ski at night!"
"What else can you do during the polar night?" Isabel asked.
"Well, many people go to concerts and cook meals together. People like to go ice fishing and ice skating. We can even feed reindeer."
Isabel laughed. "I could never do some of those things in Florida! But it must be hard to live with so little sunlight for three whole months."

"Some people find it difficult. They use special light boxes that give the effect of the sun. Other people take vitamin D pills. Not getting enough sunlight can cause a lack of vitamin D." Erik shrugged. "I love the polar night."
"What's summer like?"
"Great," Erik said. "From May to July, we have the midnight sun. It stays light all day long. You can go hiking or swimming in the middle of the night."
They went into a cafe to get warm.
"So, what would you like to do while you're here?" Erik asked.
"Actually . . ." Isabel took a sip of her steaming hot chocolate. "Everything sounds fun!"
Isabel's month in Tromsø flew by. She went skiing and ice fishing. She sledded down snowy hills!
On her last night in Norway, Erik came by. "I have a surprise," he said. "We're going to drive outside the city for a show."
Forty minutes later Erik pulled into a parking lot. They got out of the car and followed a trail to a dark field. People were standing there, staring up at the sky.
"Whoa!" Isabel gasped. Waves of green light danced above. "The northern lights!"
Erik grinned. "They're caused by particles from the sun entering Earth's atmosphere. You can see the show best when you're close to the North Pole."
Soon they were driving back to Tromsø. "Ready to return home to warm, sunny Florida?" Erik asked.
Isabel shook her head. "Nope! I love the polar night. It's beautiful—and fun!"
"Ah-choo!" Arthur sneezed loudly into his hands.
"Arthur, don't you have a tissue? Please sneeze into your arm, not your hands," Mrs. MacPhee said.
"Why?" Arthur asked. He held up his hands and wiggled his fingers. "I can catch the sneeze droplets better with my hands."
"Cold germs spread very easily―especially after a sneeze," the teacher said. "Every time you touch something, you could spread your cold germs."
"Eww!" Sarah said, leaning away from Arthur.
"Rhinoviruses are the most common cold viruses," Mrs. MacPhee said. "They can live for up to 24 hours outside of the body. They can even live on things like computer keyboards and doorknobs."
"So if I use the computer after Arthur, I might get a cold too?" Sarah asked.
The teacher nodded. "Even hours after Arthur used it."
"'Rhinovirus' sounds like 'rhinoceros!'" Cody said.
The teacher laughed. "The word 'rhinovirus' comes from the Greek word for 'nose.'"
"I've had four colds already this winter," Sarah complained.

"Most children get eight to twelve colds a year," the teacher explained. "There are over two hundred different viruses that cause the common cold. Adults get only two to four colds each year. That's because they've already been exposed to many of the viruses."
Cody put up his hand. "I read that sneeze droplets can travel almost two meters."
Sarah frowned. "That's disgusting."
"How do you think we can avoid catching a cold?" Mrs. MacPhee asked.
"Stay two meters away from somebody who is about to sneeze?" Cody guessed.
"That's not always possible," the teacher said. "Any other ideas?"
Sarah pointed to the sink at the back of the classroom. "Wash our hands with soap?"
"Excellent idea, Sarah," Mrs. MacPhee said. "We should wash our hands in warm, soapy water for at least twenty seconds. This gets rid of the germs."
Arthur put both hands over his nose and tilted his head back. "Ahh . . . ahh . . ."
The other students all leaned away from Arthur.
Arthur put down his hands and grinned. "Just kidding. I wanted to see if you were paying attention."
"It's almost lunchtime. Everyone, please line up to wash your hands." Mrs. MacPhee smiled at Arthur. "Arthur, maybe you should go first!"
Welcome to Mawsynram, India! This village sits high in the hills below the Himalaya Mountains. Mawsynram is famous for something: it's the wettest place on earth!
Every year Mawsynram gets over 11,870 millimeters of rain. That's enough to fill a rain gauge as tall as a four-story building! Ninety percent of this rain falls from April to September.
What makes Mawsynram get so much rain? An annual wind system called a monsoon. There is a wet monsoon and a dry monsoon.

During the wet monsoon, the wind comes from the southwest. It brings water from the ocean. Clouds form and travel with the wind. But the Himalaya Mountains block the clouds over Mawsynram. So rain falls . . . and falls and falls!

So much rain makes Mawsynram green and beautiful. But living in this monster monsoon is not easy! There is frequent flooding and a lot of mud. There is too much water to raise crops. So people must grow and store food during the dry season. Or they buy food at the market. They must also store wood for fuel.

Oh, and the pounding rain makes a lot of noise! People use grass to soundproof their tin roofs. Clouds often drift through houses and everything gets wet! Women weave grass umbrellas so that people can work in the rain. These umbrellas cover the body—just like a turtle's shell!
Even with those umbrellas, getting around Mawsynram can be tough. Roads wash away. And wooden bridges rot within a few years. So people build "living" bridges.

First they lay bamboo across streams. Then they tie tree roots onto the bamboo. The roots grow across the stream and into the soil on the other side. The bamboo rots away. But the roots form a living bridge. The oldest living bridge is over five hundred years old!

Whew! After so many months of rain, people are ready to dry off. The dry monsoon starts in the autumn. Dry desert air blows in from the northeast. The rain finally stops and the water drains away. But the dry monsoon brings a different problem. Now people have too little water—in the wettest place on earth!
Almost everyone has heard of the Inuit people. We live in Canada, Russia, Greenland, and the state of Alaska.
Many of my people are hunters, and we move around a lot. We hunt seals, walruses, and whales. But it is not easy to find these animals. Sometimes it takes many hours. Sometimes it takes many days.
During winter, we need a warm place to sleep when we go hunting. My ancestors invented the igloo. Igloo means house. It is a house made of snow. My father and I will show you how to build an igloo.

First, you need to make snow blocks. The snow must be hard or it will be difficult to make an igloo. Cut bigger and heavier blocks for the bottom. Shape the snow blocks with a spade. The tops of the blocks are cut on an angle. This way, they form a dome when you put them on top of each other. Arrange the blocks in a circle. Use two blocks to make the door, and another for its roof. Dig out the snow on the igloo's floor. Now there will be more room inside the igloo, and it will be warmer too.

For the top, use smaller blocks. Keep throwing snow out as you go. Now the igloo looks like a small dome. Go inside the igloo. Place the last few blocks from inside. Next, fill in all the cracks with snow. Then, use your hand to smooth the igloo walls.
The igloo's door should be on an angle too. It should be dug deep to keep the cold air from blowing into the igloo. This also stops unwanted visitors like bears. Now our igloo is finished!

My father makes a hole in the roof so we can cook. Don't worry! The fire will not melt our igloo. As the hot air from the fire rises, the cold air outside immediately freezes it. The snow blocks become harder.
We use whale fat to make a small fire. Fish is my favorite. We sit on animal skins to eat. It is very warm and cozy inside our igloo.
After a good night's sleep, we are ready to hunt again. For the Inuit, making an igloo takes only a short time. With an igloo, we can survive the cold winters.
My ancestors invented a clever and unique shelter to stay in when we are hunting. How proud I am to be an Inuit and to sleep in an igloo, the amazing snow house!

Last Thursday, just before dinner, Steve Jones and his sister were playing in their front yard. It was a warm spring day and they were enjoying themselves in the sun. All of a sudden, the sky started to get dark. Then it became even darker.
"It looks like it’s going to rain," said Steve. "We’d better get inside."
Just then the wind really started to blow. As the children reached their house, a large lightning bolt struck nearby. Then they heard thunder boom. Within minutes it was raining very hard.
"This is the biggest thunderstorm I have ever seen!" exclaimed Steve. "Look! Now it’s snowing!"
"That’s not snow," said Steve’s dad. "That’s hail. We’d better turn on the radio. There might be a tornado coming."

"The National Weather Service has issued a tornado warning for Madison County in Texas," said the voice on the radio. "This could really be a bad one. You’d better move to a small room in your house and get away from any windows. If you have a basement, go downstairs right now."

Then came the wind. It roared so loudly that Steve thought a train was driving through their kitchen. Dad had to shout at the top of his lungs to tell the family what to do. "Everyone! Go to the basement now!" he shouted. Dad turned off the electricity and Steve turned off the gas. Then the family hid in the basement.
The noise grew louder and louder. Then the house started to shake. They could hear the glass smashing and wood breaking. It was terrifying. Steve and his sister started to cry.
"What’s going on?" Steve shouted.
"The tornado is hitting our house!" Dad shouted. "Don’t move! Cover your head with your hands."

After a few terrible minutes, the sound quieted down and the house stopped shaking. Steve and his family carefully climbed out of their basement. Their house was a complete mess. All of the windows had been smashed to pieces, and things had been blown all over the house.
Outside, things were just as bad. The family car was upside down, and most of their trees had been knocked down. Debris was scattered all over the neighborhood. Steve started to cry.
"Everything we own is gone," cried Steve.
But Steve’s dad replied, "That’s not true, Steve. We’re all alive and safe, and that’s what is most important."

Tornadoes are very powerful and can cause great destruction. When warm, moist air collides with cold, dry air, the air does not mix well. If warm air gets trapped below the cold air, it tries to push itself up. As the warm air moves upward, it spins around extremely quickly.

The mixing of cold air and warm air causes a thunderstorm. Usually the thunderstorm just dies out, but sometimes the air rotation is very strong. Most tornadoes are very small and don’t cause much damage, but some tornadoes can be very dangerous.

There are three kinds of tornadoes: weak, strong, and violent. A weak tornado will not hurt you if you are inside your house, but a strong tornado can be very harmful. However, if you are in the basement of your house, you will probably be okay. Violent tornadoes are the worst. They are the real killers. Even if you are in your basement, you may not be safe from one of them.

The tornado that hit Steve’s house was a strong one. The wind twisting inside it was about two hundred kilometers an hour. That is twice as fast as a car drives on the highway. Steve and his family are alive and safe today because they listened to the tornado warning and took refuge in their basement.
After several weeks of hard work, Steve’s family managed to repair their house and return to their usual life. But Steve never forgot the day when the tornado hit his house.
An announcement came over the radio. " Taekuk crew, you are now free to move around."
"Yippee!" shouted Jinwook.
"Jinwook! Stop fooling around! We have lots of work to do!" Captain Peter scolded.
But this was Jinwook's first time in space. He was too excited to work.
"Now that we're in space, you can take your pressure suit off," Linda said with a smile. Jinwook could not believe it! It was his dream to travel in space. He was about to begin his space adventure!
Jinwook and the crew worked hard for several hours. Soon it was time for Jinwook's first meal in space.
"It's not easy to eat in space. Eating in space takes practice," Adam said.
"What do we eat?" Jinwook asked.
"We can eat just about anything, but the food has to be made into a sticky paste," answered Captain Peter.
Dinner was spaghetti!
Mealtime in space is often playtime. Adam's favorite trick is playing with his drinks. In space, water floats in the air in big drops.
"What's this for?" Jinwook pointed to the Velcro on his trousers.

"That's Velcro. If we don't hold onto things, everything just floats around in space. So we use Velcro to hold things down," Adam explained. "Even this food tray has Velcro strips underneath. It can be attached to the wall! Watch!"
"Do we float because there is no gravity in space?" Jinwook asked.

"Gravity? Of course there's gravity," answered Adam. "But in orbit around Earth, there is very little gravityㅡalmost zeroㅡand you don't feel any weight. That's why it's so easy to move. That's why you can float in space. Look at Captain Peter," said Adam. "He's running on the exercise machine. Floating inside the space shuttle, we hardly use our bones and muscles at all. So to stay healthy, we have to exercise every day," he explained to Jinwook.
"It's bedtime," Captain Peter said.
Adam gave Jinwook a sleeping bag. "Make sure you attach your sleeping bag to something." Jinwook nodded, but he was too excited to sleep.
Jinwook stayed up and looked out into space. "It's so amazing to be in space," he said to himself. Finally, Jinwook fell into a deep sleep.
Jinwook was having a wonderful dream. He was telling his family and friends about his space adventure.
"Ouch!" he cried suddenly.
"Jinwook! I told you to attach your sleeping bag to something," said Captain Peter.
"Wake up, Jinwook! Jinwook!"
"Wake up, Jinwook!" his mom was saying.
"Captain?" Jinwook called out sleepily.
"Captain? It's Mom, Jinwook! You're late for school!"
"School? There's no school aboard a spaceship," said Jinwook, waking up.
"Spaceship? You must have been dreaming." His mother laughed.
Jinwook picked up his book. "What happened to Captain Peter and Linda and Adam? Where are my Velcro trousers?"
Jinwook spread his arms out. "Last night I had my first space adventure," he said excitedly. "Do you know what I want to be when I grow up?"
"Let me guess—an astronaut?" His mother winked.
"Look how big its feet are!" Eric pointed.
"How did they find all the bones?" Dana raised her hand. All the kids in the class were looking at a dinosaur exhibit.
"Do you want to know a secret?" Miss Bennett, the museum guide, said in a low voice. "Those are not real dinosaur bones!"
"But . . . but . . . but," Eric stuttered.
"So dinosaurs never existed?" Carol asked timidly.
"Of course they existed!" Miss Bennett laughed. "But those bones are not the original bones. Follow me and I will explain."
The class followed her into another room.
"First, who knows where those bones came from?" Miss Bennett asked.
"From dead dinosaurs?" Eric answered.
"They come from fossils!" Carol said.
"You are both right. The dinosaur's dead bones turned into fossils."

Miss Bennett switched on a projector. She pointed at the dinosaur on the screen. "Look at this dinosaur. Usually, when a dinosaur dies, it decays or another animal eats it. But sometimes the dinosaur is buried before it gets destroyed. Slowly the flesh and skin of the dinosaur rot away. Only the bones are left. Then more and more mud and sand cover the bones. The mud and sand, which are called sediment, press down on the bones. The sediment has water in it. The water has minerals. The minerals soak into the dinosaur bones. Slowly the bone material is replaced by the minerals. The bones become hard rock. Now they are fossils.

This process takes a very long time. It takes thousands and thousands of years for the sediment to form heavy layers. These heavy layers turn into sedimentary rock around the fossils. So most fossils are found in this rock."
When the slide show was over, Miss Bennett gave everyone a slab of clay.

"Let's try a simple experiment," she said as she held up her hand. "Place your hand on the clay. Pretend that your hand is a dead dinosaur covered with sand and mud. Press down on your hand and imagine it is being covered by more layers of sand and mud. Imagine the sediment keeps pressing for thousands, even millions of years!"
"Ouch! My hand hurts, Miss Bennett!" Eric said.

Everyone laughed, and Miss Bennett continued her explanation. "It took many years for the dinosaur bones to become fossils. Finally scientists dug the fossils out of the sedimentary rock. They had to be very careful not to break the rock. After they cleaned the rock, what did they find?" asked Miss Bennett.
"A fossil!" everybody answered.
They all held up their slabs of clay. On each one was a handprint.
"Your handprint is not your actual hand," said Miss Bennett. "But we can still see that it was a hand. In the same way, fossils are not the actual bones of a dinosaur."
"Is that why you said that the dinosaur bones we saw are not real?" called out Eric.
"Yes, you are right." Miss Bennett nodded.

"Remember, the original bones are replaced by rocklike minerals," Miss Bennett explained. "So a fossil is just a model of the original bone, like your handprint. And the dinosaur bones in the exhibit are models of the fossils."
"Thank you, Miss Bennett," the children said together. "We learned a lot today."
"Come back anytime!" Miss Bennett waved. "There is still more to learn about the world of fossils."
Hi, I am a balloon. Have you ever wondered where balloons come from? Well, today is your lucky day. I am going to give you a tour of a balloon factory. Come with me!
Look at all these colors. In this factory, they make 25 different colored balloons. Do you think you can name 25 different colors? Try it! It's not easy.
Where should I begin? I guess the best place to start is at the beginning. In this room, the workers prepare all the ingredients that we need to make balloons.
This white goo is called latex. This is what all balloons are made of. It doesn't have any color yet, but it soon will.

Now let's go to the production line. This is where the gooey mixture is turned into balloons. In this factory, they make many kinds of balloons: long balloons, round balloons, small balloons, and multicolored balloons.
Let's look at some of the machines. This machine gives each balloon its shape. This machine heats the balloons until they are dry. Then, that machine removes the balloons and puts them into bins.
This is a big factory. Can you guess how many balloons it makes each day? One thousand? One hundred thousand?
This factory makes one million balloons a day!
Oh no! One of the machines is broken and the production line has stopped. This is very bad. But not to worry! The repairman will fix it in just a minute.
The repairman must work fast. If he doesn't, people may not have balloons for their birthdays or picnics.
In this factory, all the balloons must be perfect. This woman makes sure that every balloon is good. She makes sure the color, weight, and shape of each balloon is just right.
The next room is very bright and colorful. Look at all the balloons! Here the workers stamp words onto the balloons. She is stamping "Happy Birthday." Over there, he is stamping "Happy Halloween."
Last stop! In this room, the workers sort the balloons and put them into small bags. The men put the balloons onto the truck. The balloons are ready to go to the stores.
Well, I had fun telling you all about the balloon factory. I hope you had fun too!
There once was a boy named Thomas who lived just down the street in the house with the red bricks. Thomas didn't care about the environment, and he never recycled his garbage.

One day an old wizard smelled an awful stench while he was working in his basement. He walked upstairs and outside and kept following the scent until he found himself in front of Thomas' house. He stopped out front and looked at the garbage piled up on the curb. He shook his head with disgust and said, "Look at all this trash! Thomas must learn that he should not waste his garbage."

The wizard pulled out his wand and put a spell on Thomas' house. Now, every time Thomas threw away good garbage, it would talk to him. The spell would not go away until Thomas stopped wasting his garbage.
That night Thomas noticed a mistake after he printed his homework. Without thinking he threw the paper into the trash.
"Hey! What are you doing?" said a voice.
"Who said that?" Thomas asked.
It was the paper! "You are wasting me! I am not garbage," it said.
"Yes, you are!" Thomas pointed. "There is a mistake printed on you."
"Look at me. I still have one blank side," said the paper.
"What can I do with that?"
"You could draw a picture. You could write a note. You could play a game. You could do your math homework."
"Wow! I never thought about it before," said Thomas.
"Well, you should start thinking about it more often. I am precious," the paper explained. "A tree had to die to make me. Don't waste a tree by throwing me away! You must learn to recycle."
The next day Thomas went to the kitchen to make his lunch. He ate a peanut butter and jelly sandwich with a glass of milk. Then he put the empty peanut butter jar into the garbage.
"Excuse me! Take me out of here right now!" said the jar.
"Why? You're garbage," said Thomas.
"No, I am not! You can use me for something else."
"Something else? Like what?"
"I can hold your marbles. I can hold your pennies. I can hold your candy. I can hold many small treasures," the jar answered.
Thomas' head was spinning with ideas. This was the strangest thing that had ever happened to him. Talking garbage! But he agreed that the jar was very useful, so he put it in a safe place.
Later that day, Thomas ate some oranges and threw the orange peels into the trash can. It happened again.
This time the peels started to talk. "Stop! We do not belong in here."
"Why not? You're definitely garbage!" said Thomas. "There is no way I can reuse you. You would smell bad."
"No, we are very special garbage. We go into the compost bin," said the peels.
"What is a compost bin?" asked Thomas.
"A compost bin is a special box where you put all your vegetable and fruit scraps. In the spring, you put us into your garden, and we help your flowers grow."

Thomas did not understand why his garbage was talking all of a sudden, but he started to understand what it was saying. He took the orange peels out of the trash can and put them into the compost bin.
The next morning, while Thomas was getting dressed, he accidentally ripped his shirt as he pulled it over his head. Since it was an old shirt, he took it off and threw it into the garbage.
"Where am I going?" asked the shirt.
"You are an old ripped shirt, so you are going into the garbage. I'm sorry, but there is nothing I can do with you," said Thomas.
"You are wrong, Thomas! You can use me as a rag. I can wash the floor. I can clean your bike," explained the shirt.
Thomas was amazed. It seemed that everything that used to be garbage still had a job to do─even orange peels and ripped clothes! He had a whole new understanding of his trash.

Thomas learned a lot from the talking garbage. He did not want to cause environmental problems anymore. That afternoon he went around the house and looked in all of the garbage bins. He found everything that he could reuse and put it all in a special place with the rest of his treasures.

The next week Thomas' garbage bag was very small. Even the garbage man was impressed when he came to pick it up. Thomas had saved all of the used paper, all of the empty bottles, and all of his old clothes. He had even made compost out of his fruits and vegetables! There was hardly anything to throw away.

However, the garbage man was not the only person who was amazed by Thomas' new habit. The old wizard had also seen the small bag of garbage on the curb that day. During the night, when everyone was asleep, he walked by Thomas' house enjoying the fresh air. He smiled and laughed as he looked toward the house.
"Ha-ha! Thomas, you have learned your lesson. You have learned to save your garbage, so I will remove the spell from your house."
Rava: Hi, my name is Rava the Lava. Careful! Don't touch me. See, I am one thousand degrees Celsius. I'm hot! This is my friend Java the Lava. She's hot too.
Java: Hi there! It's nice to meet you.
Rava: We are not from here. We come from a very different place.
Java: Hey Rava, let's tell them how we got here.
Rava: That's a great idea! Today, we came out of a volcano. Before that, we were magma, which means melted rock. We are from deep in the earth.
Java: Let's go have a look! When you travel down into the earth, it gets hotter and hotter. Thirty kilometers down, all the rock is melted.
Rava: Down here used to be our home. We lived here with the magma. Everything is very hot.

Java: When rock turns into magma, it makes gas. It becomes very crowded down here. So the gas pushes us up to the surface. The gas and the magma try to find cracks in the earth's crust. We push everywhere until we find a crack.
Rava: Hey guys, I found a crack over here! When we find a crack in the crust, we climb up it.
Java: We rise and we rise, pushing through the earth.
Rava: It is hard work. But soon we are almost at the surface of the earth.
Java: When we get to the top, we all work together and push through the earth's crust.
Rava: Push! We push so hard that we fly up high into the sky.
Java: Whee! We have made it to the surface.
Rava: It is much cooler here. Ah, I like it here.
Java: Up here the gas, the air, and the magma all mix into one. Together they make lava.
Rava: That is how we got here today. Most people do not like lava because we destroy their cities.
Java: But we did not know there was a city here!
Rava: Watch out! Get out of the way! We can't stop.
Java: Now we are beginning to cool down.
Rava: Soon we will become rock. Then, we will be part of a volcanic mountain.
Java: Volcanoes make very large mountains.
Rava: Many mountains were made by lava that cooled into rock.
Java: There are the Smokey Mountains in the eastern United States.
Rava: There is Mount Kenya in Africa.
Java: And many, many more.Sometimes volcanoes erupt in the ocean. When this happens, a new island is made.
Rava: The islands of Hawaii were made from a volcano. Long ago, magma pushed through the earth's crust under the ocean. When the lava cooled, the new islands of Hawaii were born.
Rava: We must say good-bye. We are becoming hard. Soon we will be rock.
Java: Good-bye!
Rava: So long!
